utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Niemann, how do we start? Do we start with your motion or...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Mr. Turone will argue the motion on behalf of the Prosecution, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic and I appear on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia. I appear on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic together with my colleague Michael Greaves, attorney from Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, I am Salih Karabdic appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, together with my colleague, Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman, I appear here today on behalf of Esad Landzo, together with my co-counsel Ms. Cynthia McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Turone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, the motion filed on October 1st by the Prosecution seeks leave to call as additional expert witnesses Dr. James Gow and Professor Constantin Economides, on the basis of paragraph 2, sub-paragraph 4 of your Honours' order issued on 25th January. We can read in that subsection of the aforesaid order that for good cause shown the Trial Chamber will allow testimony of expert witnesses where notice of such expert testimony is given after the required date. So the original required date was in the early months of this year; at that time the Prosecution designated two expert witnesses, Dr. Calic and General de Vogel. Then in March, the first one, Dr. Calic, was examined and cross-examined in this courtroom. Then, on July 4th, in a previous motion, the Prosecution informed already the Trial Chamber and the team colleagues of the Defence that it may call additional witnesses to prove the international character of the armed conflict in Bosnia Herzegovina and to prove that the victims in this case were protected persons pursuant to Article 2 of the Statute, concerning the very narrow scope. As a matter of fact, the judgement in the Tadic case had been issued in the meantime, on 7th May, establishing some legal parameters for proving such circumstances. Now the new designation of expert witnesses is filed by the Prosecution for the following reasons, which in our submission constitute good cause according to paragraph 2, sub-paragraph 4, of the 25th January order. First of all, as I was saying, the elements of Article 2 offences were first established in the aforementioned opinion and judgement in the Tadic case on 7th May, including the requirements for proving the existence of an international armed conflict and the quality of protected persons according to the Geneva Conventions. Although the Prosecutor has given notice of her intention to appeal that decision in this respect, however, the parameters established by the Tadic Trial Chamber anyway suggest a different focusing on these relevant issues. Moreover, subsequent to the testimony of Dr. Calic new facts, new information on the internationality of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia and the protected status of the victims have come to the knowledge of the Prosecution, again, on these two very narrow subjects, and the Prosecution is now seeking to present this new information through Dr. Gow, a military expert to be called instead of General de Vogel, and Dr. Calic, as we know, was not a military expert, keeping in mind the parameters established in the Tadic decision as for internationality of conflict, an issue for which Dr. Gow is deemed to be a suitable expert witness. Finally, as far as the nationality issue is concerned, on 13th June this year the Trial Chamber, your Honours, have already granted leave to the Defence counsel of Mr. Delic to designate an expert witness on the law of citizenship of Bosnia. The Defence counsel wrote in his motion he had no objection to the designation of a similar expert witness by the Prosecution, and this is what the Prosecution intends now to do, through the designation of Professor Economides, again keeping in mind the parameters stated in the Tadic decision for protected persons status, with particular reference to Article 4 of Geneva Convention IV. The designation and the CV of Dr. Gow and Professor Economides were filed on October 1st, together with this motion, and in the following days the Prosecution provided all the esteemed colleagues of the Defence with a statement of the areas of their testimonies. So this is my legal argument on the motion. Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May I have any reaction on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will discuss the two witnesses separately, and in both cases rather briefly. With regard to Dr. Gow, the Prosecution has pointed out in its motion to seek leave to call additional expert witnesses, and Mr. Turone has pointed out this morning that subsequent to the testimony of Dr. Calic "new facts and information" -- and I am reading from their motion: "... new facts and information on the internationality of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia and the protected status of the victims have come to the knowledge of the Prosecution. The Prosecution seeks to present this new information to the Trial Chamber". It is not clear, from reading that paragraph, the nature of that new information. If it is in the form of documents, we have not been provided with those documents and under prior orders of this court should have been at least by this time, it seems to me. If it is not in the nature of documents, it could be quite helpful, in terms of the preparation of cross-examination of this witness, to be informed by the Office of the Prosecutor what that new information is. Beyond that, with regard to Dr. Gow, I have no further comment. With regard to Professor Economides, the Trial Chamber should know that basically what we have been provided are two small paragraphs containing very sparse information about who this man is and what the nature of his expertise might be. We can only conclude from looking at those, at that information, those two small paragraphs -- I am holding it up so you can see, your Honours, the extent of what has been provided to us. You probably have a copy of it. It is about five and a half lines of typewritten material. It appears that Professor Economides is being offered to this Trial Chamber as a legal expert, being brought here to tell your Honours what the law is. In most places that would be an improper use of expert testimony, unless the legal expert was being called for the purpose of establishing foreign law. That is not my understanding of the purpose of Mr. Economides, but that he is being asked by the Prosecution to come here to tell your Honours what international law is. I believe that is the exclusive province of the Trial Chamber, to determine what the law is, based upon the advice and arguments of counsel in the case, and is not a matter that is subject to expert testimony. Based upon that reasoning, I object to Mr. Economides being called. There is precious little before this Trial Chamber which would even permit you to conclude that he has any expertise at all and that he properly falls within the category of an expert witness. The Prosecution has presented virtually nothing. There is virtually no information about what it is that they expect his testimony will be; but the best we can conclude is they are offering him as an expert on international law, which I think is not an appropriate use of expertise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Very quickly, first, I mis-spoke something yesterday. I said Mr. Gow had published 15 articles in Jayne’s' publication; it turns out to be nine. I apologise for the factual mistake, to be right upfront. Secondly, let me limit my remarks as to Professor Economides. As the Prosecutors properly noted, we offered an expert in Bosnian law, because courts need expertise to know what the law of a foreign nation is. There is no showing, anywhere that I know of, that Professor Economides is licensed to practice law in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he has ever practised law in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he has the slightest idea what the citizenship laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina are. Just, for instance, he would be just -- have the same kind of expertise speaking about British nationality law or American nationality law, or a nationality law of the People's Republic of China. Because he lacks this expertise in the area where I believe that the Trial Chamber probably needs some expert testimony, I do not think he will be helpful to the Trial Chamber. For that reason, until they get an expert in Bosnian law, I do not think that there is any need for an expert on this, and I would object to this particular witness testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Delalic we would adopt the arguments put forward by our friends Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, what is the situation for Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. First of all, to avoid unnecessary repetition, I fully endorse the elaboration of the reasons given by my learned friend Mr. Ackerman, but I would like to add the following: it is quite true what has been said regarding Professor Gow and his literature, which is really minimal. But we also lack something important, when this witness was proposed to assist the Trial Chamber in dealing with all the problems required to pass a fair judgement, and that is that we do not know at all what the Doctor's dissertation, of this gentlemen, was, nor do we know the title of that dissertation. I have not been able to establish that he is an expert for the area of the former Yugoslavia, because the question of Bosnia-Herzegovina is linked in symbiotic connection with the former state, so anyone who is not really knowledgeable about the legal and constitutional affairs of the former Yugoslavia cannot know what is important for the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was later recognised as an independent state. Therefore, I too would like to object, regarding the proposed expert witness; and I believe that we should bring before the Trial Chamber a person who would synthesise both the positions of the Prosecution and the Defence, so that there should be no doubts as to that person's expertise and all other credibility of that individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us hear you, Mr. Turone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. About the information which Dr. James Gow is supposed to give to this court, I would like to emphasise that the answer to the question raised by Mr. Ackerman is at least in part answered in the statement of the areas of the testimony of this expert witness, which we filed in due time. We said that Mr. Gow will describe the armed conflict that occurred on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the Konjic municipality, in 1992, between the Yugoslav People's Army and the Bosnian armed Serb forces on the one side and the BiH army on the other side, and so on. But more in General, we should say that the narrow scope of the expert testimony of Mr. Gow is anyway included in what was the area of testimony which was supposed to cover and which was many months ago given to the Defence lawyers, which was supposed to cover the other military witnesses we had designated in advance, which was General De Vogel. So in a way I would say that the new designation of the military expert James Gow is somehow a substitution of the previous military expert we had designated then, and the different focusing which is suggested by the new Tadic case law intervened in the meantime suggested to us to narrow the scope of the military testimony and file a new designation in the person of Mr. Gow. On the other hand, we have to underline that all what Dr. Gow wrote on this issue can be easily found in his bibliography, and I would suggest that between October 1st and November 3rd, which is the date when Dr. Gow would probably be called to testify, the esteemed colleagues of the Defence have the time to read what this expert witness wrote on the narrow scope of internationality of the conflict and status of protected persons in the former Yugoslavia. About Professor Economides. I would say that in the CV of Professor Economides the main feature concerning this expert witness is the fact that he is a member of the European Commission for Democracy and Law of the European Union and in that capacity he was the reporter of this Commission on the issue of state succession, of state succession, which is the real issue coming out in this trial. On the issue of state succession and nationality. Whatever was prepared by Mr. Economides in the framework of this European Commission is easily to be found in Brussels in among the material of the European Commission. Furthermore, he is also a member of the United Nations International Law Commission. I would also add that in this case it is not really a matter of being expert witness exclusively on the law of Bosnia on citizenship. This is certainly also one of the aspects, but the matter coming to our attention is the matter of nationality issue under the Geneva Conventions, and particularly with regard to the succession of states, the states' succession. So this, I think, is my answer to the objections of the Defence. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a couple of quick things. Firstly, the Tadic -- although the Tadic Trial Chamber issued its decision on 7th May, applying the law to the facts of that case, the law itself is nothing new. It is based on both the Tadic appellant decision from, I believe, October 1995, maybe November 1995, and the ICJ's opinion in Nicaragua v US, which is 1987, 1988 case, things almost ten years old. Secondly, as I pointed out to the Trial Chamber yesterday, I have spent many hours trying to find things out about Mr. Economides on the Internet, which is a very good source of information, and this Commission that he is a member of. As I pointed out to the Trial Chamber yesterday, all I could find on Professor Economides was one reference to being a member on a European Commission Against Torture. I found absolutely no references to a European Commission for Democracy and Law. Clearly, he has written a substantial amount of information as a Reporter of this Commission. I do not know that we can get our hands on it and digest it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first thing I want to respond to is the way in which Mr. Turone skilfully avoided responding to the major point that I was trying to make. That is the statement by the Office of the Prosecutor that there are new facts and information on the internationality of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia and the protected status of the victims that have come to the knowledge of the Prosecution. I specifically requested in my initial remarks that in order for this Trial Chamber to make a proper decision regarding this matter it would seem to me that the Trial Chamber would have to have some indication of what these new facts and information consist of. If they consist of documents they should have been turned over to us quite a long time ago. Mr. Turone did not respond directly to that whatsoever. I think that needs and requires a response. With regard to Professor Economides, the response was very much what I had suspected, and that was that he is going to be proffered to you as an expert on international law, which I think is improper and will not be of any help to such a learned Trial Chamber, which probably, with the experience that the three of you have together, would outweigh anything Professor Economides could offer by several tongues, I would think, based upon looking on his CV and that of the Honourable Judges sitting on this Tribunal with regard to international law issues. I therefore suggest to the Tribunal that before you can make a decision regarding either of these matters, you need more information. Perhaps you have sufficient information now from which you could decide that you do not need to hear from Professor Economides. With regard to Professor Gow, I think you do need more information to make that decision which should be provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor. If this Tribunal determines that they will permit Professor Economides to be called then I would like leave to make additional remarks to the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is possible, Economides' both publications are published, both sides will be satisfied with his Commission. I do not know. Do you have any contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, one short contribution to make. It concerns the position of Professor Economides, with respect to your Honours' position. The reason why evidence of what international law is not admissible in this court might be taken from a useful publication which states pithily what the position is. That is Juberre's Law of South Africa, volume 9. This is the law of South Africa, but it applies, in my submission, equally here: "It is not permissible to lead expert evidence on a point law. The court notices it, not because it is a matter of common knowledge, but because the court the organ of state entrusted with the functions of declaring and applying the law." That short sentence identifies what your role is. If Mr. Economides comes along and gives expert evidence on what international law is, he is effectively becoming a member of the Trial Chamber. That is not permissible. Interestingly enough, in the law of South Africa international customary law is considered to be incorporated in that state's law. It should be judicially noticed and expert evidence to prove it is in fact inadmissible. It cites a number of authorities for that proposition. In my submission, if what Professor Economides is going to come to do is give evidence about what the international law of a succession of states is, as opposed to expert evidence of the law on citizenship in Bosnia, it is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the court reporters' system, because of the way it is set up, seems to be substituting my name for Mr. Economides on occasion, and that could be confusing in the record as Mr. Greaves has just disparaged my expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will grant the application. Let us hear Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to Professor Economides, he was the Reporter to this Commission, the European Commission for Democracy and Law. We have -- my colleague, Ms. McMurrey, this morning has had a discussion with the Office of the Prosecutor regarding that report. It was learned that the Office of the Prosecutor in fact has a copy of that report. When Ms. McMurrey asked Mr. Niemann to please furnish us with a copy of it, he refused to have any conversation with her about it, refused to respond to her inquiry and basically ignored the request. I wish these matters could be worked out without bringing this to the Tribunal's attention, but if Mr. Niemann is going to refuse to even discuss such issues with us then we must bring it to your attention. Due to the short time between now and when he is likely to testify, rather than ask for an adjournment once we find this, it seems to me that in the interest of making things move along with this Tribunal that it would be totally appropriate for the Tribunal to order the Officer of the Prosecutor to give us a copy of that report and any other writings they have of Professor Economides, otherwise we will have no choice but to seek an adjournment for the purpose of gathering up these documents and being prepared to cross-examine the Professor. We have somewhat the same problem with regard to Professor Gow; however, based upon your ruling this morning, we will endeavour now to start marshalling the documents necessary to prepare that cross-examination. We will hope that we can do that without requesting any kind of adjournment from the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is yet another example of misconstruction and accusing me of things which have not happened. When I was asked about this I said I do not have it and I do not know, but that I would make inquiries. At that moment, I then instructed Mr. Khan to send an e-mail message upstairs to see whether or not information could be obtained, because I did not know of it in relation to the report and I did not know the telephone number that I was also requested of. This is just a lie. They were here, she heard it, now it is being totally misrepresented. This sort of behaviour is going on time and time again in this Chamber. It is most regrettable and most unethical. I will produce a copy of the e-mail, your Honour, as soon as I can have it produced by the printer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond, since Mr. Niemann just called me a liar in court. What happened was I did ask Mr. Niemann for the telephone number and he did talk to Mr. Khan and said he would try to arrange for us to get the telephone number of the expert. When I asked for the report he did not respond to me that he would provide me with the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This type of thing should not be continuing here. What has been told to the Trial Chamber is that he has refused to react to your request. That is what we have just been told. This is what he is trying to reject. That is not completely the position. Well, I think in the ordinary manner of co-operation I am sure they will try to give you the sources of the information; if you can get the reports and if they can find it for you they will do so. I do not think there is any difficulty in co-operating in matters of this nature. I think this is the end of this application. We grant the application. Thank you. Next we go on with your witness. General ARIF PASALIC (continued) Examination-in-chief by MR. NIEMANN (continued)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may sit. Morning, General. Remind him that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. General, yesterday we were speaking about Sefer Halilovic and his position of Chief of Staff during the period of 1992. In relation to his position, was he ultimately responsible for prisoners of war detained by members of the Bosnian Herzegovina army at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic is Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, was my superior officer. All issues regarding action and combat and prisoners of war were linked to his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that would include dealings with prisoners of war, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was responsible to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command in all regards, for all issues, including also the matters of dealing with prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And would this apply to other immediate subordinates of Sefer Halilovic in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when it came to dealing with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell my own opinion. I think they were all in the same position towards the superior officer, who was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. They all had the responsibilities and their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, when it came to visitations at camps or prisoner of war facilities by the International Committee of the Red Cross who was it that was authorised to permit inspections in the hierarchy of the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period from April 1992 up until the establishing of the Crop, I did not have prisoners of war that were based in prisons or other premises. I did not have any camps. I turned over my prisoners of war to the headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council. But in order for the ICRC or any other international organisation to visit any of my institutions or establishments I had to have the accord of my superior officers; that was the staff of the Supreme Command. In that case I would be allowed to allow the visitation of any international organisation including, the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would that apply, so far as you know, to other Commanders of such army groups as Tactical Groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say my own opinion about that. I think that would go also for all the other subordinate groups and commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in relation specifically to the Celebici complex, when that was being utilised as a prison facility, did that ever come under your responsibility, at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for Celebici, which is a complex where those people were isolated, I only learned about that towards the end of November. That is when I established a committee that would have to investigate the matter. I was never at Celebici or had any responsibility over that complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was it that you investigated it then, General? I mean, I know you were not there, but why did you cause the investigation into it, if it was not a matter under your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started the investigation when I became the Commander of the 4th Corps with an order issued on 17th November, 1992. As that case happened at Konjic somewhere from the 20th November onwards, I established, as I have already told you, a commission that had to investigate and find out the facts of what happened in Konjic. That commission informed me that at the warehouse of the former JNA at Celebici there was a certain number of people who were isolated there. By contacting those people and by contacting the people who ensured the security of the place that there were persons who died for various reasons, people that were not alive. I decided that it should be found out what was happening and I was informed that investigations should be started, linked to the missing of those people or to their death. That is when I started proceedings against those people as it is stated in that Act for the starting of criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. General, I think there may have been some confusion in my question. What I was asking is: was there any time when the Celebici camp came under your responsibility? Specifically, did it come under your responsibility after 17th November, when the 4th Corps was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the establishing of the 4th Corps, because the facilities at Celebici were physically lying within the area of my responsibility, I decided to have a look into it and when I did so I wanted that the camp be disbanded and that those people be sent in the prisons which had such a purpose. I did not have time to look into the camp, as you call it, that is of Celebici. These were these isolated persons. I considered those people, persons were not combatants so I only asked for those people to be transferred to other centres, and for the situation to be -- the matter to be investigated into.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, during the period of 1992, did you know or come to know a person by the name of Esad Ramic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met Esad Ramic in the same period when I met Mr. Zejnil Delalic and the others. That is when I arrived to Konjic. I think that at that time Esad Ramic was in the staff of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Konjic. I do not know whether he was just a legal officer, or the head of the staff. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did he stay in Konjic for the whole period of 1992, or did he subsequently leave Konjic, in terms of the place where he was stationed in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1992, I found him in Konjic in the staff of the Territorial Defence and later on when the Corps was established he became part of that Corps as one of the operational officers of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, those are all the questions I have. I just wish to check with the Registrar, if I may, whether Exhibit 141 was -- I tendered it, but was it accepted into evidence for the truth of its contents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was admitted yesterday into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the Trial Chamber did not accept 141 for the truth of the matters therein but for the relationships. As I recall that distinction was made by Judge Jan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My friend is quite right, it was tendered for a limited basis. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all you have with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We will proceed in this way. First counsel for Mr. Delic, second counsel for Mr. Mucic, third counsel for Mr. Delalic and fourth counsel for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If the Defence would not mind, because my colleague would want to put some questions before cross-examination starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask, General Pasalic, if it is possible to assist the Tribunal in the following: General, when you talk about aggressors or aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, I am primarily referring to aggression by the former Yugoslav People's Army, as we call them, the Serbian-Montenegrin aggressor. Later in 1992, in the second half of the year, there was aggression also by the Croatian Defence Council. But in this case I was mostly referring to the aggression by the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: And could you explain to me if some paramilitary groups were also part of this aggression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me as a citizen of Bosnian Herzegovina and an officer of the Territorial Defence, all those who were outside the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and outside the law and the armed forces were paramilitary formations. The only legal military formations, according to me, were the Territorial Defence and the HVO. The remnants of the former JNA, the army of Republika Srpska, which we did not recognise, were for me paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: General, when you use the word "Chetnik", who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately I use the term Chetniks, members of the former JNA and the army of the so-called Republika Srpska, now an entity, have in certain designations the Chetnik prefix. Historically this dates back to the Chetnik movement in Serbia, Kosta Pecanac and onwards, whose ideology was a greater Serbian nation and the formation of a greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: That means according to your opinion there were attacks coming from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina and coming from inside Bosnia-Herzegovina against the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attacks were carried out by formations of the former Yugoslav People's Army and other paramilitary formations established in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled by Serb nationalists. But there were units coming to Bosnia-Herzegovina from the territory of Serbia, such as the Uzice Corps, which was in the south of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and which was attacking Mostar and other formations from the former Yugoslav, that is from Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have been very useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Thomas Moran and I -- your Honour, I think I am on the wrong channel. Now I am hearing English rather than French. Let me introduce myself. I represent a man named Hazim Delic, and I am going to ask you some questions and they are going to be fairly general questions, and maybe some of my colleagues will ask a little bit more specific things about this. But I am going to ask you questions about military organisation, command structures, military justice, things like that. As a little preface, just so you know where these questions are going to be coming from, I spent 21 years in the active duty in reserves in the United States army and I have recently retired, so I think we may be talking somewhat officer to officer. The first thing I would like to ask you about is the command relationship between the HVO and the TO in the period from, say, April of 1992 through about November of 1992, just in general terms. At any place in the command structure, did the HVO share a common commander with the TO or the army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the organisation of the defence and resistance against the aggressor, TO units were formed, led by the republican staff of Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Parallel with that and maybe a little earlier, I do not recall the date, units of the HVO were formed, learning a lesson from the war in Croatia. Those units, that is HVO units, and TO units at first acted in co-ordination against the aggressor, that is the former JNA and Serbian-Montenegrin aggressor. However, the headquarters of the HVO was formed by Janko Bobetko as commander of the southern theatre of war in 1992. I think it was in March or April; and it was an independent command in relation to the municipal TO staff. The command of the TO was in Sarajevo and the command of the HVO was in Posusje and in Siroki Breg. The relations between these two commands, I am not competent to say, and I am not familiar with the way it functioned, but I know that in the field I was Battalion Commander. We did co-ordinate with the HVO in the territory of the Neretva River valley in Herzegovina, based in Mostar. That co-ordination consisted of mutual consultations, agreements, and conduct of combat operations against the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So, General, when you were a Battalion Commander in early 1992, and there was an HVO unit operating in your area of operations, did you, for instance, have the authority to call in that HVO commander and say: "you work for me. Take that hill"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before engaging in operations, we would agree on who would be the Commander of that particular operation. If I was Commander of a Battalion I had my own area which we had delineated between us and the HVO and if we were fighting an aggressor and an HVO unit was attached to me then it would come under my command. If I was participating with a part of my unit in another area of the battlefield and the HVO unit was in charge, then my unit would be subordinated to the Commander of that HVO unit. That was the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So the practice was that at some time before the battle the HVO Commander and the TO Commander and possibly their staffs, and possibly other people, would get together and decide who will be in charge of this operation, and another operation tomorrow it might be that someone else was in charge. Is that a fair assessment, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of a particular combat operation or task, but if talking about the territorial responsibility, the area was also decided, in some areas there were BiH army units or rather TO and in others HVO. So that it did occur that one could not have parallel Commanders, but certain areas of responsibility were designated and each one was in command of his subordinated units and received instructions from the HVO command in one case and in the other from the TO command. So it was a highly complicated system of control and command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And I suspect that in your logistical operations, supplies, weapons, ammunition, gasoline, vehicles, it was the same kind of complicated relationship between the TO and the HVO, is that a fair assessment, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The logistics for subordinated units and command was set in very complicated conditions. There were no rules. It was the conditions that dictated the rules. We in the TO received supplies from our own logistics bases and some we had to obtain ourselves. We were assisted at first by the HVO, and this applied mostly to clothing and food. In some cases, we did assist one another with some equipment -- military equipment, but this was limited in scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Well, of course, at that time for both the HVO and the TO there were, I suspect, some severe shortages of everything, from weapons to combat boots. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were absolutely short of everything. We did not have uniforms, boots, clothing. We did not have sufficient weapons either. The HVO was quite well supplied, but I am not familiar with their sources of supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And I suspect that Commanders for both the HVO and the TO and the supply of logistical officers for both the HVO and the TO were rather jealous of what they had and they wanted to keep what they had for their units, so sharing things became a complicated system of negotiations. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As Commanders of the TO and the HVO we did not have many disputes amongst ourselves over that. We had logistics problems because we were short of things, and there was the question of supplies, was further complicated by the blockade. But naturally, each side kept what they had for themselves, and what they needed in the event of fresh operations against the aggressor and they took great care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And between the headquarters of the HVO on one side and the TO on the other, would it be common for you, for instance, to have a liaison officer in the HVO headquarters to co-ordinate your activities, your logistical problems with the activities, operations and logistical problems of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mostar as Battalion and Brigade Commander I did have a liaison officer in the HVO command in Mostar. That officer co-ordinated in a sense our common interests. Also in the area of logistics, but in other areas as well, between these two components, that is TO units and HVO units, I do not know how the Republican staff and the main headquarters of the HVO co-ordinated. My task, assigned to me in September 1992, was with Jasmin Jaganjac and Anto Prkacin, as HOS Commander, to go to central Bosnia to prepare the ground for the establishment of a joint command. We were in the territory of the Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica, but unfortunately we did not ever establish that joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: I know you are not familiar with the operations and the co-ordination between the two in the Konjic area because you were -- in the spring and summer of 1992 -- because that was outside of your area of responsibility. But would it be unreasonable for the civilian authorities in the municipality to appoint someone of some stature in the community to act as a mediator between the TO and the HVO, so that they could work out their differences and work together in a smoother way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards the Konjic municipality, visiting Mr. Zejnil Delalic once on the front, I dropped by with Jasmin Jaganjac to the headquarters of the HVO of the Konjic municipality. We then discussed our mutual relationships and our co-operation. I saw we were co-operating. There were cases that the President of the municipality would appoint somebody to co-ordinate with the HVO and the HVO would also send people to co-ordinate with us, to have negotiations and discussions with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And just because that person who acts as a mediator or liaison between the HVO and the TO that does not necessarily give him any command responsibility in and of itself does it, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what kind of responsibility he would have. It depended on what the responsibility was assigned to him by the person who appointed him. I had my own representative in the headquarters of the HVO, Adem Zulovic. I was the one who gave him assignments as to what he should do in the HVO command, and which are the areas in which we can co-ordinate with the HVO. This co-ordinator of mine was responsible for military matters. We were a military organisation, as was the HVO command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And your representative in the HVO command, your liaison officer, was not a commander, was he? He was a liaison officer to, a staff officer to help you co-ordinate your activities with an adjacent unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He had no authority to command. He had the authority to represent us, the TO, in the HVO command, and to work on the co-ordination. He did not have any executive command functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: General, since you have mentioned executive command functions, I would like to talk about that and the theory of command if we could, just in general terms; as a Commander and a former Commander I am sure that you are familiar with it; but is it not true that in any army in the world, any military organisation in the world, a Commander, simply because he is a Commander, has special responsibilities and special authorities that some other person even of equal rank who was not a Commander would not have, would lack? That was a poorly framed question, General; if you do not understand it, I will be happy to break it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both in the former JNA and the TO and in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina the Commander is the most responsible individual for the overall situation in the subordinate units, and not only for the situation, but also the consequences and the directions of future activities. But the term of "executive command" applies to officers who directly issue orders to perform specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. For instance, in armies that I am familiar with a Commander is responsible for everything his unit does or fails to do. He is responsible for making sure that his men are fed, that they are equipped, that they get their mail, that -- he is responsible for promotions, demotions. That would be the same in the former JNA and the TO, and the current army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it not, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When you are talking about a Commander, he has the right to command. The other persons in his command have specific responsibilities, assistants, officers, et cetera. But they have no right to issue orders. Every order has to be verified by the Commander. There is the right to execute a task, that is one right, and the right to issue orders is another right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And sometimes, General -- and this is going to tie in, I think, to the concept of a Tactical Group. Now, a Tactical Group is something that I have very little familiarity with. But let me -- I would like to discuss it a little bit, and as a preface I may draw some parallels to the organisations that would be used in a NATO army. As part of your training as an officer, did you become familiar with the organisations of NATO armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did study the NATO alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Good, because I now think we can talk on the same sheet of music, General. As I understand what a Tactical Group is, it is a unit that is formed either based on an existing unit, or units are added to it, or just out of the whole to perform a specific task, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general terms, Tactical Groups are temporary military formations, formed to carry out specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So, for instance, in the military that I would be familiar with, we might form a task force, where there might be an armoured Battalion that would need an infantry company to perform a mission, so that infantry company would be sent to the armoured battalion for this one mission. Is that generally what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If talking in general terms about Tactical Groups, they may be of mixed composition, various units, of various sizes and various purposes. In NATO, one of the largest groups that was ever formed was in the Middle East in Kuwait. You had armed forces from all NATO members, an enormous Tactical Group that was assigned the task of Kuwait. It was enormous -- you did not call it a Tactical Group, it was an Operative Strategic Group. But "Tactical Group" is at the left of tactics where you have companies, platoons, detachments which are grouped under a single command to carry out a specific task; in this case, the defence of the municipality of Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor, Vakuf from the aggression of the remnants of the former JNA and the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: One of the things I am familiar with, and I would like to know if both the current BiH army, the TO and the former JNA would operate this way, if I were to send an unit to another -- to aid another unit, to set up a task force or Tactical Group, just because that unit is assigned to a Tactical Group, does not mean -- in and of itself does not tell you the authority of the Tactical Group Commander over that individual unit, would it? Let me give you an example. I will tell you what I am looking for, General. It might be possible, for instance, to just give a Commander operational control of another unit, so that he could say "take that hill" or "hold that road junction". But that Commander may not have any other responsibility for that unit. That Commander who has operational control may not be responsible for feeding the troops, or for their -- making sure they got their pay. Would that kind of thing be possible under a Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are using other terms now. You are talking about subordination and attachment. It all depends on how it was regulated by the person giving the orders. If he has given you a unit to watch over a particular facility then he will tell you what your responsibilities and competencies are in relation to that group. Do you have to feed them and supply them, or will somebody else feed and supply them. We are talking now very generally. If we are talking about Tactical Group 1 the Commander of the Tactical Group 1 and whoever appointed him must know the competencies and the responsibilities he assigned to the Commander of the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is 11.30 and I have quite a bit more to do. This is our traditional time to take a break. Would it be appropriate to do it now, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we will break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, General, see you in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness is brought in, there are a couple of matters I wish to raise, if I may. Your Honours, an order was issued by subpoena for General Ramic to attend. He has arrived and been here since Tuesday night -- Monday night, I should say. We do not expect that we will be in a position to call him today, which would mean either he has to go back -- and if he stayed I think he would probably be here for a very long time. So our position on it now is that we have decided that, with your Honour's leave, if your Honours are disposed to release him from the subpoena, we would envisage that he goes back, and I do not think it will be necessary for us to call him. I should say, however, that he has agreed to speak to the Defence on the same conditions that General Pasalic agreed to speak to the Defence, namely as long as a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor was present. If he goes back and if your Honours are disposed to release him, the Victims and Witnesses Unit would like to organise travelling for tomorrow morning. I raise it at this stage, if the Defence are anxious to speak to him, then could it possibly be organised for this afternoon, after court, and he can be made available then with a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. I raise that for the information of counsel. That being so, and if your Honours were disposed to release him from the subpoena, we -- General Divjak -- we understand that it is not going to create a difficulty for him to stay over, and there is the custodian of records. If there is time this afternoon, we would like to call the custodian of records, because from the point of view of the evidence-in-chief it is not anticipated he will be a long witness. He may -- it may be that he goes over to the next stage, to next week, but if that is so, I do not think the compass of his evidence is that broad. So if I just may mention those matters, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been informed, I do not know how good the information is, that we were to meet with the General today at the lunch break. Is that correct? That is General Divjak, I am sorry. I was misinformed, misunderstood what was being said. I am sure we can arrange to meet General Ramic after court tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Finally, your Honours, I did undertake to obtain copies of the e-mail that was sent this morning. I hand up those three copies. Finally, your Honours, I have to say that the information that sought by the Defence by Mr. Ackerman in relation to Professor Economides is still being sought and as soon as we obtain it we will make it available. I hand those to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you intend to apply to withdraw the subpoena against General Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, on the basis I think the evidence we have taken so far is sufficiently broad enough. It does not look as though we can get to him towards, at the earliest, the end of next week, and possibly the week after. It is so long down the track we do not think it is fair to hold him over here for that period of time. We believe we can proceed without his evidence, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do we have to call him to say we are withdrawing the subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can undertake to convey that, or, if you want, I can call him. It is a matter for your Honours how you wish me to deal with it. I thought it was inappropriate for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you think it is sufficient, although I would have thought the proper thing would have been a proper motion. I think it is sufficient for an oral application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours would prefer a motion to be filed, I can undertake to form one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can inform him that if you decide to call him he should be available on those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Issued at the subpoena. Now you are supporting his request that the subpoena be withdrawn, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. That is the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are indicating that we withdraw the subpoena against him -- has been withdrawn formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will provide a draft of that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I would like to ask, first of all, if my learned friend Mr. Niemann could give us the precise order of the persons that will be heard as witnesses next week so that we could prepare ourselves for it. The second point is that I know that I am not authorised to discuss the subpoena, whether it should be annulled or not, but since these past days I am not only in the media, which my colleague has commented upon, but also in front of this Trial Chamber we have heard lots of things related to the subpoena, so if you will allow me, if I can, as an attorney from Sarajevo, and these people come from Sarajevo, may I ask you to annul the subpoena towards those persons regardless of the fact that some of them have already testified, and the others will testify. I think that this would be a correct and very honourable decision of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure after they have appeared and given the evidence there is any point in withdrawing the subpoena. You already asked them and they have said they were prepared to come voluntarily. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For those who have given evidence their subpoena is spent. There is no need for it. Actually I do not know how to decide the argument about which of them is telling the truth; at the time we order the subpoena we had certain facts which we relied upon; contrary facts have appeared. So be it. The subpoena is spent, they have given the evidence. We do not have to bother about that. It is not any offence against them that they answered the subpoena. We have not gone into the issues to know the type of information which the Prosecution had before these subpoenas were issued, and I do not think we need bother about that at this stage. But for those who normally would now give evidence, if there is sufficient evidence, as Mr. Niemann has withdrawn this, I suppose he would withdraw the subpoena with respect to anyone who he believes does not really require a subpoena to be here. So, I do not see why you should bother so much about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would only like to say a few words. We have discussed many times about the legal knowledge, the legal culture, in our areas, and also in the countries where you have been judges for many years, and subpoena is considered, is perceived to be some kind of a punishment towards those people. Maybe some kind of a statement made by the Trial Chamber, something like you have just said, maybe or would have the effect of clearing those people, because they have got some kind of, like a negative effect, the subpoena that remains on them. Because all those people consider it will be an honour to come and testify in front of this Tribunal, and not how it is perceived now, as some kind of a stain in the reputation that it is perceived in Bosnia-Herzegovina now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will discuss with the Prosecutor and see how it could ameliorate whatever effect it might have had on those on who subpoenas are still outstanding. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Niemann has presented a memorandum or an e-mail, or something, to the court just now. I cannot imagine why. It seems to reopen a matter that I thought that this court had put to rest, and I think it is inappropriate for him to have done so; but in as much as he has done so, I now feel a need to point out to the court that the e-mail request for six copies of the requested document was only transmitted apparently from this courtroom after the issue had been raised with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, have you any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I presented it because I said to your Honours I would. The relevant time is not the one where the six copies are asked to be brought into court it is the one beneath it, which shows the time 10.13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 10.13 time is absolutely consistent with what Ms. McMurrey informed me, that he said he would try to provide the telephone number. The 10.54 time when the copies are requested is consistent with that not having been done until it was brought to your attention that he had refused to discuss that matter with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is all right. I think we hear. Let us lay it to rest at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was my belief it had been laid to rest earlier. I did not want to raise it at this issue; Mr. Niemann raised it again, so I felt I had a need to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we get the witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly inform the witness that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. General, something I forgot to mention when I first started asking you questions, I will just do it now on behalf of myself and the rest of the Defence lawyers, we would like to express our condolences for the death of your brother. Sir, that having been said, let me go back to where I think we were at the time of the break. I would like to chat with you a little bit, because frankly, the situation, the military situation that you were involved in, is something that happens very, very rarely in history, which is where a country has to try to form a country and an army and a military and a defence structure, while, at the same time, it is conducting military operations, actual operations. I suspect that in the period from, say, April 1992, through probably November, when you formed the Corps, that the military situation was a very confusing situation; that lines of command and control were unclear, missions were unclear, it was -- who was in charge of what was unclear, that it was probably a pretty confusing situation militarily. Is that a fair assessment, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, based on the military situation, you had to probably put people in positions of authority and responsibility who lacked experience and training to normally be in those positions. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And that the relationship between the civilian authorities and the municipalities and the military authorities in the same area would probably also have been quite confused during that period of time, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So, basically, what you were doing was trying to form a defence structure while you were actually defending your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Let me jump back, for just a second, sir, to the Tactical Groups. I was thinking about it over the break and there were a couple of things I was a little confused about; if I am confused, I suspect I am not the only person in the courtroom that is. Again, as I understand a Tactical Group, it is a temporary headquarters that is set up to carry out a particular mission. It is to do one thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have said that the general term "Tactical Group", we understand to be a temporary formation of certain units at the left of tactical units which are platoons, companies and battalions, in order for them to perform specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: When you say "task", I am saying "mission". I think we are saying the same thing, are we not, to do one thing? General, if you would look, there is a lady in front of you; that is a court reporter, and there is another lady over there; that is a court reporter. She has to write down everything we say. She cannot write down a nod, so I am afraid, sir, you have to say "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So the record is clear, the answer to the last question -- you nodded in the affirmative, a yes, is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So, for instance, if a Tactical Group had the mission of breaking the siege of Sarajevo, that would be all that that Commander would be worried about. He would not be worried about, you know, commanding logistical units in Mostar, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It depends in what sense he was appointed Commander. If the commander of a Tactical Group was appointed to break the siege of Sarajevo, then one should state clearly who is to supply him, who has to co-ordinate, who acts in operations with him, and so on. That means that the duties of the Commander of the Tactical Group have to be spelled out. The term "breaking the siege", is a sentence that in fact encompasses a series of actions, and procedures. Is the breaking of the siege going to last one day, 10 days, 20 days? So time has to be spelled out. How long the mission will last, in what way they are going to perform that mission, and what are they going to do after the mission has been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So without looking at the order, and without knowing exactly what the mission and the parameters of that Tactical Group were, you, as a general officer, would not have, would not have the knowledge to say who was in charge of supplying these troops or who was in charge of making sure they got paid, or got their mail, or whatever. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Sure I can. I would be happy to. As an outsider, someone who is not directly involved with either the Tactical Group or the higher headquarters which created the Tactical Group, even as an experienced general officer, without knowing the exact orders that were given, creating the Tactical Group, setting up its mission, defining which units are in it, defining which tasks every one has. You, as an experienced officer, would not know what that Commander's responsibilities were, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I issue the orders, I would have to know that; and if somebody else was issuing these orders to him, in that case, I do not necessarily need to know that. So the one who establishes the Tactical Group knows which orders and tasks were issued to the Commander of the Tactical Group and to the whole Tactical Group. I do not know whether you are satisfied with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Basically I am saying that someone that is not the Commander establishing the Tactical Group or the Commander of the Tactical Group itself, someone who is outside of that chain of command, would not necessarily know the parameters of the authority given to the Tactical Group Commander, would he? Because they can be different for each Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: General, I am going to, with your permission, slip to another subject. I am going to refer to it, as I am frankly trained to refer to it, as military justice. When I refer to military justice, I am referring to the ways that the military imposes punishment on people for various crimes, associated with or committed while in the military. Anything from desertion and absence without leave to murder. Okay. General --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: In the military that I am familiar with, and frankly they are the western militaries, there are some wide differences in how different armies handle military justice. For instance, the German army has a very narrow scope of its military justice, while the American army has a very broad scope. One thing that is generally consistent that I have seen is that military justice and the authority to do those kinds of things rests with Commanders and no one else. Is that the same way in the Bosnian army and the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And one other thing that is very common in the western armies, and I am curious whether it was that way in the former JNA and the TO and the current army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that different levels of Commander would have different responsibilities and different amounts of authority to discipline troops. That would be the same; for instance, a Company Commander would not have the same authority to discipline the troops and apply military justice as, say, a Division Commander. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And another thing that is very, very common, specially in the American army, and I guess I can do it best by example, I think all armies have a thing that they would call "Company punishment", where some minor infraction of the rules -- a Company Commander would deal with a minor punishment. In the British army I believe they call it "Company punishment". In the American navy it is called "Captain's mast"; in the American army it we call it Article 15, because it is from Article 15 of our Uniform Code of Military Practice. For example, a military Commander under the law has the authority to take away half a month's pay for two months from a person. He can fine that, he can give him so much extra duty. I am sure that kind of thing exists in the Yugoslav army and the former JNA army and the Bosnian army as it is set up today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former JNA, there was the competence, the authority one had in issuing a military justice. The Commander of a platoon would undertake disciplinary measures for the breaches of discipline of his soldiers. The same was true for the Commander of a Company or a Battalion or of a Regiment. But if a soldier makes a criminal offence, something that needs criminal proceedings, then lower ranking officers cannot deal with it. In that case, the courts have to deal with it, of higher instance. I agree that all the officers, the Commanders and the leaders had specified duties which they had to do or measures they had to undertake in case of breaches of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: One of the things that I have seen, again, and mainly in western militaries, I want to know if you have this in either the BiH or the TO or in the former JNA, is that in some cases a higher Commander has the -- in fact, in all cases, a higher Commander has the right to hold to himself authority that would normally be given to a lower ranking officer. Again, let me give you an example. We were talking about Article 15s, Company punishment. Uniformly in my army, the post Commander, who was probably -- who was a general officer in almost all cases, withholds from his subordinates the right to give Company punishment to commissioned officers, Lieutenants and Captains and higher ranking officers. We are not going into specifics; did that kind of thing occur in the former JNA also, and the TO and the BiH army? Again, for instance, you as a Brigade Commander could say, "I will be the only person who is authorised to punish people, no one else can"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that was prescribed in your duties, then you have that right. But if it is not prescribed in that way, you will be usurping those rights. For each level of Commander, it is clearly defined what their competencies are, so you cannot assume any responsibilities which are not prescribed. I am saying this based on the experience of the former army. In the TO, these regulations were not fully established, and I could not punish my subordinates unless I had the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So again this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you are talking about these punishments in peacetime. I think the level of punishment changes when the army is engaged in defending or -- during hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I can tell you how both would work. The two I am familiar with is the Bundeswehr, the German army, and my army. In the Bundeswehr there are a lot of changes when hostilities break out; in the American army there are very few changes. It remains pretty much the same. I think the one difference is, off the top of my head -- some of the maximum punishments go up. Espionage in time of war is different from spying during peacetime. But for the power of the Commander, as I recall the only additional power that an American Commander would have in wartime is that he can put a soldier in irons and feed him bread and water for seven days. Does that answer your question, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure that the witness quite grasped your question. If I understand you, are you suggesting that a higher Commander can stop other officers under him exercising their powers of punishment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is -- your Honours, I was trained to say exactly the thing you are in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is what perhaps you wanted. Whether that practice exists in his own army, is that not what I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think that is absolutely correct, your Honour. I think Judge Karibi-Whyte probably phrased the question a bit better than I did; as a higher Commander, can you tell your Company Commanders, "I am going to punish people; if you want someone punished, I have to do it"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could do that, but I would have to tell my subordinate officer that, that I would be the one to punish and that that is within my terms of reference and I would have to report my superior that it was I who had punished the offender.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And had the authority to do it. The big thing I was getting at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that authority is prescribed. If my superior gave me permission to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine. So your superior, as a Brigade Commander, was a Corps Commander. Your superior was the general staff in Sarajevo, the Supreme Headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And the Supreme Headquarters in Sarajevo could give to you the power -- they could -- all the power you had, all the authority you had, in all forms of command, from manoeuvre to training your troops, to military justice, came from the Supreme Headquarters in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the staff of the army, or the Supreme Command, as it was later called, headed by the Chief of Staff. They would, by written and oral orders, regulate my competencies. If I wanted to take any disciplinary measures, or institute criminal proceedings, then I would have to inform those responsible of the same, or ask for permission. I did not have to ask permission for a minor infraction, but if it was a major offence I would have to ask for an explanation from my superior as to what I should do and what the procedure should be that I should follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So in all areas of command, you were regulated -- you had no more authority than what the Supreme Command gave you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to repeat that the rules of conduct were not regulated and published before 1993 for the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and these prescribed the general principles and rules of conduct. In those rules, issued in 1993, the general responsibilities of Commanders, leaders and officers were specified. Until then, we did not have such a document, but the Supreme Command would occasionally, through written orders and oral instructions, indicate how we should behave in certain situations, just as they gave us assignments. So they instructed us how to treat military equipment, captured equipment, how to treat captured persons, deserters, how to behave in various conditions that we found ourselves in, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And so, without knowing, either from you directly or from your Commander, what orders were given to you, I would not know what authority you had as a Brigade Commander. Is that fair? Again, this is in the period of confusion in 1992, that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: General, one last area, if the usher could be good enough to show the General Prosecution Exhibit 137. I believe that is an order detaining certain individuals. General, I do not want to talk about this in detail, I am just using this as an example, okay. I will be right upfront with you why it is that I am asking. My client and three of the other -- three of the four defendants are charged with illegally detaining people. I want to ask you a series of fairly short, fairly specific questions about the authority of people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, and some of it is going to have to do with the law. I know you are not a lawyer, but -- if you do not feel competent to answer, that is fine. In Prosecution Exhibit 137, you signed an order detaining 13 people for 30 days, so that an investigation could be carried out. Was that a legal order under the law in effect in Bosnia-Herzegovina from, say, April 1992 through the time you issued this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is the report that I sent to the Supreme Command of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not an order. In this report, I inform my superior that I have decided to detain a certain number of people for up to 30 days. Those were my legal powers at that time, as a Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: So, General, it was within the authority of the -- I was about to say in the authority of the authorities; that is a horrible sentence. But it was within the power of people in authority to detain persons suspected of crimes while the crime was being investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the Commander of a Corps, I was entitled to detain, from one to 30 days, persons, in order to investigate matters, because those people could have abandoned the territory, they could have deserted, something could have happened to them and the like. I was within my rights as Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. I agree that I think in almost every legal system in the world where there is evidence to believe that a person has committed a crime, the competent authority can order them detained for some period while it is investigated.
