And when these people, these 13 people, were arrested, they were delivered to a confinement facility of some kind. I will give you an example; my client was actually imprisoned in the Celebici camp, pursuant to your order. You would expect the people that were running the confinement facility to hold those people in custody until such time as you ordered them released, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here "up to 30 days". The commission conducting the investigation could have released any one of these persons when they assessed that the investigating procedure has been completed. All of them were not detained for 30 days; some three, five, 15, I cannot say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: What I am getting at is the commission that was set up to investigate had the authority to order these people released, but you would expect the people in charge of the jail, prison, whatever other confinement facility, to hold them in custody either until the end of the 30 days or until the commission ordered them released, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commission proposed for how long people would be held in custody, and as these were professionals, lawyers, in the commission. They would propose to me whether the proceedings would be started against somebody and when, continued legal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, I am not sure whether I understand what you are putting. I remember you started with questioning whether he had the powers to do what he did; is that what you are still putting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Now where I am going is whether the people who were actually confining these people had the duty to do that or whether or not they had some responsibility to go behind his order and to determine whether or not the General's order was a legal order, a wise order, or whether they are just to follow the orders of the General and the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why not put that straight to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: General, do you understand what I was asking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is whether the persons who were complying with his orders can use their discretion to disobey. That is what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. Would you expect them, presuming it was a lawful order, as you say it was, would the people actually confining these prisoners have the discretion to disobey your orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I have not fully understood. He cannot have the discretion not to obey orders. I was the one who formed the commission and who assigned its tasks, so I am also the one who controls the commission. If they do not follow my orders I will find a substitute, I will have somebody dismissed from the commission. And I determined this detention on the basis of the decision of the Supreme Command. This is a report. I reported to the Supreme Command. The Supreme Command confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: I agree with you that that is the way it should work. One last question, I think, and then I am done. The commission that you set up, you said was run by professionals who knew what they were doing and were investigating -- had a pretty broad scope of investigation, did they not? Their competence, the mission that you gave your commission, was to investigate everything that happened in the Celebici camp, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My commission consisted of my assistant for legal affairs, and the other assistants who were professional to a degree, and, taking into account what you also said, they were not always absolutely qualified, but we had what we had. Because I confirmed that point that you made before. The task of this commission was not to fully investigate everything that had happened in Celebici. Its task was to elucidate what Celebici was, and then it is the next stage of the criminal proceedings, which is up to the judiciary to carry it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOM MORAN
utterances.text: And your commission, while it was investigating what Celebici was and the disappearance of some people, did a good job, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did the job it did. If it was not a good job, one might talk about it. But I think that it accomplished its task to the extent to which they could in view of the conditions under which they were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: General, I thank you very much and I hope you have a good trip back to Sarajevo. Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, may it please the court. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Olujic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Before I put a number of questions to you which are important for the Defence of my client, as opposed to my previous learned friends, Mr. Moran, I would like to ask you to answer my questions a little more slowly, or rather to wait for my question to be interpreted into one of the official languages of this court, and those are English and French, and to only then proceed to answer my question, so that all the parties in the proceedings and also for the benefit of the record, we are able to follow the questions and answers properly. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, allow me to put a number of questions which you will find easy to answer, but which certainly need to be put in order to elucidate certain points. In the course of the examination-in-chief, by my learned friend Mr. Niemann, you said that you were a career officer, as the saying goes. In other words, you went through all the different levels of training in the former JNA in order to, in a more mature period of your life, to enrol at the military academy, which you graduated from successfully, and began to serve. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember describing myself as a "career officer". I called myself a professional officer. I think that was the term I used, that my profession was an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am satisfied with your answer, yes, a professional officer. Will you please tell me whether you are familiar with the situation in Konjic in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it was difficult and complicated, rather like it was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, according to the constitution of the former state, the SFRY, did anyone have the right to sign capitulation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: As a professional officer, do you know that the death penalty threatened anyone who might dare to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean according to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the teaching of political education, were troops taught that no one may sign the capitulation in the JNA, and other things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: General, was this studied at the military academy as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were there also interpretations given at the military academy between the Yugoslav laws and the international conventions signed by Yugoslavia, or rather did you study the fact that Yugoslav laws have greater importance than the international conventions to which Yugoslav was a signatory? In other words, that the Yugoslav laws were applicable to every one in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In military institutions, both in the secondary school and in the military academy and other military schools of the former JNA, we studied the constitution and the laws that were in effect in Yugoslavia at the time. We studied those laws, and approached them as positive laws. Those were laws of our country, at that time. We also studied the provisions and charters and conventions applicable to international law in wartime and the like. I did not make any conclusions which would mean that the Yugoslav laws at the time were in conflict with international laws. If I did identify any contradictions, I was not in a position to be able to correct them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Of course. But would you allow for the possibility that that may have existed, that you could have identified such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the extent that any other officer or citizen may have been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, General, you spent many years in the JNA. As a Muslim, did you frequently feel that you were in an unequal position in the JNA as a Muslim, and did you have occasion to hear terrible things about Muslims, jokes at their expense, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I joined the Yugoslav People's Army, I noticed that we were not treated on an equal footing. At first, I reviewed my own opinions and positions. I tried to understand what the differences were and why they existed. True, there were differences. I personally attributed them to personal qualities of individuals, and not to policies or the system, at least at the time. I did not feel I was in any kind of threat as a Muslim, up to somewhere around 1970. From 1968/70 onwards, those relationships were crystallised in the sense of increasingly pronounced contradictions, based on ethnic origin. This was particularly pronounced after the adoption of the constitution in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1974. It is true that at the time the command pyramid began to be ethnically cleansed, unfortunately to the benefit of people of Serbian ethnicity. I had all the qualities to become Commander of the airport and the airforce base. I had the highest marks in the previous five periods of assessment, that is a period of 20 years, but I was told that they were not counting on me in the command structure, because I was a fundamentalist, because I expressed my congratulations to my mother on the occasion of Bajram; unfortunately, that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your Honours, in view of the fact that it is 1 o'clock, would this be a convenient time to break and resume after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will do that. We will break and reassemble at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may remind the witness that he is still on oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. General, before the break we started, I have started with a series of questions and you have said and described, on your own example, how you were unequal in the JNA, and also that being a Muslim you were very often in a position to hear all the worst about Muslims. On the contrary, again in the period after 1970 were there, on the other side, so to speak, amongst Serb officers, boasting with Serb courage and military valour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the context with the officers I worked with, those were the officers from various ethnic groups. Among them were quite a few, maybe the majority of them were Serbs. It is true those officers always had a certain amount of boasting, starting from Kosovo and onwards, throughout the history, about the military tradition, about the Serb ethnicity and saying how good soldiers they were, how they were one of the major actors in the fighting against fascism. But I did not consider that to be such a direct attack towards the others, although it was evidence, and it is true that they have made such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When one is in the army there is also some kinds of socialising. I would like to ask you whether there were unpleasant, humiliating jokes about Muslims, whereas jokes about Serbs were not allowed to be told; that is, when those jokes were told one could be even prosecuted and disciplined, because that is -- is my allegation true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not give you a typical example of anybody being punished because of a joke based on ethnicity, but we were very cautious in telling any political jokes. It is true that there were very well known jokes about Muslims, two Muslims, Mujo and Suljo. I myself laughed about the jokes about my own people, but, however, it is true that there were mostly jokes about, more about other ethnic groups than about the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, who were the officials in Konjic before the war? Do you know who was the President of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who was the mayor of Konjic before the war. I do not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the situation in Konjic and the structure of power, who took part in the power in Konjic, before the fall of communism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of that structure in Konjic. I was aware of that structure in Mostar where I live and worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What was the situation there? Who was the President of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in Mostar the President of the municipalities were Serbs, there were Muslims, there were also Croats. These were all positions where people would change. Somebody was the President of one body and then of the other and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbs predominant by number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you exactly. I cannot give you the figures, but people always used to say that the Serbs had more power because they were also more numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, how about the companies? Were they also subject of the All People's Defence and Social Protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the constitution of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the law in People's Defence, there were companies that were declared to be of utmost importance for the People's Defence, so that some companies also in Herzegovina, in the Neretva River valley were of utmost importance for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So they were also by that fact the subjects of this All People's Defence and Social Protection, as it was called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did these companies also buy arms and organise exercises just as it was done by some political structures? Here I mean the companies of the very -- of utmost importance from that point of view that were in the Neretva River valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those companies that were of utmost or special importance for the All People's Defence had to be able to organise the defence of their own facilities, according to the law on All People's Defence. For example, the aluminium factory in Mostar, which was very important, had its own unit both for the defence of the facilities -- that means the defending of the territory -- and they also had a unit for anti-aircraft unit. Other companies in the Neretva River valleys had also the same type of organisation. One of them was very important, the factory Igman, which manufactured ammunition. It also needed its own units for defence in case of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the former state which had been called the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia did there exist a cult of partisans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean by the "cult of partisans".

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What I mean is whatever the word partisan would mean; very shrewd, very quick in fighting, in the partisan type of fighting, and specially linked to the Second World War and the organisation led by the Communist Party that existed between 1941 and 1945. Did that cult exist in the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and also in the JNA, being its army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former JNA we studied the experiences from the Second World War, that is the period from 1941 to 1945. While we studied it, we studied in our textbooks what a special way of fighting and carrying out war operations, which was the partisan way of fighting. It is true that way of conducting military operations could be found in other types of literature in the former Yugoslavia; and that partisan type of warfare was our primary type of warfare and maybe through that the partisan warfare did have a certain cult.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was determination to liquidate and to exterminate the enemy something that was praised, because that is one of the characteristics of the partisan type of warfare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The then concept of the All People's Defence as a party of the former Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted because it was considered that such a way of defending the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be efficient against any type of aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was the influence or the impact of intelligence very important in the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not speak about intelligence services and their impact on the SFRY as a state, but I know that within the military our intelligence and our security services had very prominent place. That was in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was the system of monitoring and alerting very developed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think whether you think -- what you think here --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Reconnaissance, or specially air reconnaissance, both on land and sea and in the air?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was something that had prominent place and it was developed in the army and through the All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the SFRY and in the JNA, was the Communist Party the dominant force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in the JNA there was the League of Communists. The League of Communists as a political party in power was in -- was the only party that led all the activities, personnel, selection and all other activities in the JNA; specially in the most recent period, it was specially important for the warfare and the command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether, according to the number of its members, were there mostly Serbs and Montenegrins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the command structure? The officer at the top of the hierarchy, and also in the units where I worked, Serbs were the officers that were there in highest numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was this majority of Serbs in Konjic in the -- power structure in Konjic only relative or absolute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I do not know anything about the structure of authority in Konjic before the war, so I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: General, can we agree that the conflict between the Croats and Muslims took place after the period we speak about here at this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not agree with the term "the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats". And I am a man who can state that the extremist section of the HVO performed an aggression against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately this transformed itself into conflict between two nations. I have warned against this between the 18th and 20th July when I was with Imre Agotic, who is today a General of the Croatian army and who I knew very well from the former JNA. My duty is to tell you, if you will allow me, your Honours, that at that time I had said that on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, "the very existence of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina is being denied"; that the Muslim -- the existence of Muslims as people is denied, and that one is stating that these are Croats of Muslim religion. Also the existence of the Territorial Defence is denied, stating that it is associated with the communist system of All People's Defence. What I said at that time is unless something is done conflicts will appear between the individuals from the HVO and the Territorial Defence, that is the army, and that from a conflict between individuals we will have afterwards a conflict between two nations, nationalities and that is unfortunately what happened. On 18th July, I signed the record, the minutes of what I said, and after my discussion, and I left it with General Agotic and General Tusk, who was also the head of staff in Croatia, and President Izetbegovic was informed about that, but unfortunately nothing was done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the situation. Could one say, General, that after all these events that the Serbs have restructured themselves and united in the Serb Democratic Party which was operational at that time both in the area of Konjic, although you cannot directly answer to my question, but can that be said for those areas you were familiar with, so that they restructured and then linked up with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the start of the immediate aggression I was in Sarajevo. My family lived in Mostar, my wife and my daughter, and my son was a student in Sarajevo. So I know both the situation in Sarajevo and in Mostar. The truth is that in these political differences that appeared that various people started to structure into their own ethnic political parties, specially the Serbs, which joined the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can one say that they were angry because they lost power and that the -- that is how this homogeneous situation you are talking of was brought about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the conflict, in the discussions which I had with my colleagues in the JNA at that time and when I said to my colleagues and mates in the army that I could not stay in that army any more and I was going to leave it, they told me that we will be the culprits in case Yugoslavia would fall apart. They were obviously angry because higher ranking officials of other nationalities were leaving the army, because at that time that army had lost the features I liked and I believed in, in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: General, you are a professional officer, as you say, and you were able to observe, and can one say, that on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina where Serbs, Croats and Muslims lived, that the Serbs were those who were armed in the moment of aggression. Can you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with it in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Has the JNA distributed the weapons to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had. I even know officers who were distributing weapons in Sarajevo to Serbs, in Rajlovac and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Has JNA distributed to Muslims and Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the statement that already in the spring of 1992 that reserves from Serbia arrived to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know, because I came across the reservists in Mostar over the weekend when I was going home for weekends. There were reservists from Serbia and Montenegro and the last time when I arrived to Mostar in a helicopter I saw people with a -- the cockade, with long hair, with fur hats and these cockades which simply, to me, was saying that these were formations that had great Serb aspirations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So apart from the reservists from Serbia that you could see in the spring of 1992, you also saw some Chetniks, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were special formations within the reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And how about the White Eagles, have you seen them, or heard of them being there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about the White Eagles, but I never came across them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of him, from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But he was passing through Bosnia, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a part of Bosnia, the western part of Bosnia, the Krana region.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: General, the Serbian reservists that you saw in the surroundings of Mostar in the spring of 1992, do you know whether they had -- that they were implementing the doctrine of All People's Defence and Social Self Protection, a doctrine developed in the former state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware what their doctrine was. I did not talk to them. Their behaviour was under the guise of territorial units, units intended to defend the people; but in practice it turned out to be something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that they too subscribed to the principle that no one was allowed to sign capitulation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know; probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that the Serbs could be executed? If they were to co-operate with the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were threatened by the death penalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of the type of punishment, but I know that they were not allowed to co-operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that the Republika Srpska adopted the laws of the SFRY in the area of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they accepted everything from the former JNA, except the insignia, also the law on All People's Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Republika Srpska claimed that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the aggressor against Republika Srpska within the state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard via the media that they were claiming that Muslim units were attacking, but I think this was a pure propaganda ploy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, in the spring of 1992, you described the situation as it was in terms of armament and equipment. Would it be fair to say that in the spring of 1992 there was not really time to arm the armies, because there were no weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In that period I am talking about, the first half of 1992, were unified uniforms prescribed for the troops? The ranks did not come before the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994, as you have told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have any prescribed uniforms. We wore what we had. We did not have ranks either in 1992. It was only at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 that we began to give ranks to officers and non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, General, that it was the people who carried most of the defence on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could be said. They had no other force except their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were there many spies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: General, when were the uniforms of the army of Bosnian Herzegovina actually prescribed? Do you have a date, or a period when this was determined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the rules of conduct were published we defined the uniform as a camouflage uniform, but we only defined it in legislative terms, but we did not have the resources to supply all units with those uniforms until somewhere around 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: General, in the course of your examination-in-chief you described how you acquired weapons, and that you found various ways and means to do that. In 1992 when the aggression started, did the international community assist you in arming you, or were you left to your own resources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are all familiar with the position taken by the international community, I think it is not up to me to answer that. As the Commander of a Battalion, later a Brigade and a Corps, I knew of the embargo and that the state cannot procure weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: As a high ranking officer, in 1992, with respect to Celebici, would you say that Celebici was a prison, in which case, they would come under the Ministry of Justice, or were they a camp, in which case they would come under the Ministry of Defence, or was it something in between, something undefined, neither one nor the other? I am talking of the period between May and November 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot talk about this period from May to November 1992. I can only speak of the period as from the moment I received a report that in Celebici, as a warehouse, people were being held. I never called this a prison or a camp. According to me, they were people who were contained there and how they were treated there, I am not personally aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you authorised to command, to issue commands to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my area of responsibility as a Commander of a Battalion Brigade and Corps I did not have any authority to issue commands to units and forces of the security centre, security services centre in Mostar. If any of those forces were needed in combat, we would have to get the appropriate permission from the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said that in the course of 1992 you had no rules of conduct in the BiH army, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. We did not have it in 1992 but at the beginning of 1993 it was published. I do not exactly recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I was referring to, to 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have any rules of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And in 1992 did you have any military inspection service, or did that come with the rules; that is, the beginning of 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have any kind of inspections or controls in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, in defending oneself from a far superior enemy, was there any chance or time to establish any system of supervision over camps, if any existed until November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina occurred, because it was attacked by a far superior enemy, and the people were those who organised the defence, was there any chance or enough time to create a system of supervision over camps, if any such were formed, and I am referring to the period until November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period of 1992, I had no camps or prisons in my area of responsibility. I learned about those persons in November, in Celebici. In view of the complexity of the situation, in the Neretva River valley, which in my opinion was the most singular in Bosnia-Herzegovina and perhaps the most complicated, it was extremely difficult to have full control over the situation, and I agree with you that it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In that period, the period of establishment and structuring of the army, could you, General, for instance, give orders to a group of troops to follow you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all depended on the personal authority an individual had. I had units under my command in that period who did carry out my orders. True, there were individual cases of orders not being carried out; but one could encounter certain formations which refused to subordinate themselves to a unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But, General, we have already established as fact that there were no ranks at the time. So when I am asking you this question, what I am implying is that if there were no ranks there must have been a problem when -- I was giving this example -- when, if you were to order a group of soldiers to follow you or give them any other orders, it must have been difficult. Was it complicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The system of control and command is complicated even in peacetime, let alone in wartime. Ranks are only visual signs of an officer, be he commissioned or non-commissioned, and the problems in command were extremely grave. We were creating an army under quite unique conditions. In a sense, I agree that there were difficulties in having troops carry out combat assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you took over command of Celebici, to put it that way, did you hear that there had been a conflict between Jasmin Guska and Hadzihuseinovic; and if you are aware of the conflict, was the problem in a conflict of competencies between them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that they did not get on, but what the particular -- what the specific reasons for that were, I did not know. I had a very difficult situation in Mostar, as they did in Konjic, and I had to find solutions to establish relations between the civilian authorities, the police and other structures. It is a fact that I had heard of the existence of disagreement, and difference of views between those people, the President of the municipality, the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you investigate those differences? What was the reason behind them, apart from this question of competence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not my responsibility. Those were civilian bodies of authority, and the police. I was responsible for the military aspect, for the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Celebici, to that warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did afterwards when the people who were held there were evacuated, but I was not there before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did anybody report to you there on the part of the detainees or the guards or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, I did not visit while people were being detained there. Later when we established the warehouse as a logistics base, then I did go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said, General, that you took command of a Corps at the end of 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given the order to form a Corps on 17th November, 1992, and the process of forming a Corps and a command took some time, and it went on perhaps until somewhere in mid-January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And for how long did you hold that post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you said that the rules of conduct were introduced regarding responsibilities of various functions, was disciplinary responsibility also regulated by those rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general principles of disciplinary responsibility were regulated as far as the rules of conduct of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina needed to go into that area, but we had still not received any specific rules regarding discipline and other mechanisms linked to that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So that came later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in 1994 that we started working on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, General, that in mid-1992 there were very many paramilitary formations in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, do you know when the aggression against Slovenia was committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but I am aware of when the aggression took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, General, when you deserted the JNA exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left it at the end of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was that -- did you go to Mostar immediately after abandoning the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Mostar immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, what was the relationship in Mostar in May 1992 between the Territorial Defence and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship as far as the units that the TO and the HVO had at the time was still such that it was still possible to wage a joint battle against the aggressor. But it was burdened by elements of the situation that I have already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you know Tihomir Misic, one of the organisers and instigators of the resistance against the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did know Tihomir Misic. He was killed. He was with us when we were doing reconnaissance in Mostar, some time in May, I cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was anybody accused of his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Proceedings were instituted. I do not know what the outcome was, because we made an error in the course of our reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you do not know the outcome of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My colleague Mr. Olujic has already drawn your attention to the fact that you should wait for my question to be interpreted, and you can hear the interpretation on the headphones on the table, so that everyone in the courtroom, and their Honours in particular, can follow our conversation; otherwise the two of us could quickly conduct this interview. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, I should now like to ask you something that may not be related to the rest of our conversation. Would you tell us whether it is true that somewhere in the summer of last year you told my investigator Senka Nozica that you made a brief statement for the defence of Zejnil Delalic in connection with the publication of the ID card which you spoke about in court, and after that, after I had used that statement in court, and since that statement was incorrectly interpreted in the mass media, you thought that I had used that statement incorrectly and since that date to the present you have had no contact with me. Is that true, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that I reacted, but you did not try to get in touch with me either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regardless of that short misunderstanding between us, I am confident, General, that you will answer all my questions. Let me start by apologising and saying that my military knowledge is not as good as that of my learned colleague Mr. Moran, but having lived under wartime conditions for four years and in view of everything else we have experienced I have learned that it is very important that we and the court have to know many things that are very familiar to you as a professional soldier. You will be ready to answer those questions as well, General, will you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, since you are a General in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and many of my questions will be linked to Bosnia-Herzegovina, I should first like to ask the usher for his assistance for an exhibit to be identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know -- can you tell me what this is? Do you recognise this? Please stand up, if you want to. Please stand up, you can have a look at it. Maybe I can help you and ask you: is that a map of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not look at all the details, but all the borders are rightly marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you think it is the map of Bosnia? Maybe you cannot see every single line, but this is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the witness has identified this map, I tender it as a Defence exhibit and later on we will come back to some explanations which the General should give us. Is this map admitted as evidence as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. There is nothing to object about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please could I have the number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Defence Exhibit D74/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would like to go back to certain questions you discussed yesterday during the examination-in-chief, when you gave your answers, gave your opinions and your knowledge as a person who participated in those events, and also as a soldier who has certain knowledge from his professional experience. General, during your examination-in-chief, you indicated what, according to you, means co-ordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm, General, that the term "co-ordinator" and the term "commander" represent two different notions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that the term "co-ordinator" implies a certain activity of mediation by a person between the body that appointed him and a third party, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Co-ordinator" can be what you have described; but a co-ordinator can also co-ordinate between other bodies, not necessarily only persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are various types of person, physical person and moral person, maybe that is why my question was not completely clear. So it is simply somebody who co-ordinates between various persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is somebody who co-ordinates and does activities which are given to him in the form of a task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that a person who a body had appointed for such a mediating role has no function of superiority to that body which had appointed him. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a general sense, yes, but in a specific case I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you have just said that you were yourself in a position to appoint co-ordinators, for example, Mr. Adem Zubovic. Did that gentlemen, after you had appointed him, have some superiority, a superior function, to you, over you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, it is not Adem Zubovic but Adam Zulovic, with an L.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So he could not have any superiority over you, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appointed Adem Zulovic co-ordinator between the units of the Territorial Defence in Mostar and the municipal staff, municipal headquarters of TO in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So he was not your superior but you were his superior body, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask that the General be shown Prosecution exhibit identified, marked as 67. So I would like the General to be shown the Prosecution Exhibit 67. This is a special authorisation issued on 2nd May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Authorisation giving Delalic the authority to enter into contracts, is that the document you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. General, yesterday you looked at this authorisation and upon a remark made by Judge Jan you said that there was a date of the 2nd May on this authorisation and after that you were shown the decision of the War Presidency, dated 18th May, by which Mr. Zejnil Delalic was appointed co-ordinator. General, from that fact alone, that this document is done 16 days earlier, could you confirm that this document has nothing to do with the co-ordinator mentioned in the decision dated 18th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question. I can answer about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you maybe in a different way? If you, General, gave a particular duty to your soldier today, for example, to be a messenger and he became something else two weeks later, for example went into the artillery, and if that letter appointment or authorisation cannot be retroactive and cannot influence something that was done before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are now putting me in a position where I have to speak about documents I was not in charge of at the moment those documents were issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, General, I will not insist upon that. I will only ask you whether it is true that on the document that you were shown as a decision by the War Presidency -- and I would like to ask you to have a look at it again, not at this document but the next document which I have here. It is a Prosecution exhibit, but I do not know under what number it was marked. Could you please show this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, once you will read this document, will you be able to tell us on what date was this decision made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is written here is the 18th May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the previous document, the document dated 2nd May? The heading of this document, can you tell us whether in the heading you -- it is stated that this decision is made according to the decision made on 2nd May, and that is written in the preamble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This authorisation is the authorisation by the commander of the -- by the staff commander of the municipality of Konjic, dated 2nd May 1992. The staff commander, the military staff, probably they -- what is meant here is the commander of the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is on the right-hand side a stamp here, and a signature. On such a document the President of the War Presidency is the one who affixes his signature. In the heading of this document it says, "War Presidency of the municipality of Konjic", and a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this then a document of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what is written here, it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, please, in the preamble above the words "special authorisation", does this document make reference to the document from 18th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It refers to a decision by the War Presidency which is not dated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this heading and say whether it says what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What it says is: "On the basis of the decision of the War Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on equipping obtaining and distributing war equipment the War Presidency of Konjic municipality issues the following."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So now you have read, and so I ask you, is it true that in the heading of this authorisation it is clearly stated, clearly states the decision on the basis of which this authorisation was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this decision is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this precisely mentioned authorisation is the one about purchasing and acquiring war equipment, are these duties that were given only the duties previously established about the matters of logistics that are the responsibility of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The body that issued this authorisation refers to the decision of the War Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then gives its authorisation. The authorisations only -- concern only the three points that are mentioned here, and the decision of the War Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina is something of a much wider scope.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree, General, that these three points that are mentioned in this authorisation, that they result from a much broader decision of the War Presidency, regarding the same issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if that was done along those lines, that is how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I know what you meant by your clarification yesterday. General, you said that according to the very nature of appointment and its title, the co-ordinator has no superiority but is subordinated to the body which had appointed him, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This question has already been asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I will continue now. Maybe I have already asked this question without noticing that. I could not hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can ask this question for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is necessary for your other subsequent ones you can still ask it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as the situation you spoke to us was complex, is it true that the civilian structures of authority also sometimes had the need for appointing certain persons, co-ordinators, mediators in order for certain issues to be more easily solved, in view of the complex situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that they had such needs and that had appointed co-ordinators but I am not aware of such activities of co-ordinators.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, is it also true that when a civilian body appointed somebody co-ordinator that co-ordinator could not have higher functions or commanding instructions over that body which had appointed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the military hierarchy and the military structure. What was the civilian system, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you can agree with me that in general terms a co-ordinator both in civilian and military structures should mean the same thing, a mediator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a general sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke, General, about the difficulties in overall supplying of our army after the aggression. Is it true, General, that at that point whoever was ready to acquire whatever was needed for the defence would receive certain authority, authorisations in order to do so and help defend the country. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you can agree that in 1992 many persons received authorisations to -- for the acquiring or purchase of certain goods for the civilians or for the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I also issued such authorisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would now like to show you a certificate issued by the general staff of the army which in disclosure I gave to the Prosecution last year. So could you, please, look at it and after that I will ask you certain questions. I have copies for the Chamber, and before that I would like to ask that the original copy is given by the Registry to the General. Could you please mark this copy here (indicates), because this is the original? There are also copies for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D75/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask that as I see that there is one copy -- that you have got -- a supplementary copy in Bosnian, could you please give me one back, because I have given away all the copies that I had.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I only have three copies and I need them for the judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you have the chance to read it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I meant, now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me which body is mentioned in the heading of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document, do you recognise the stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What stamp is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The general staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo, stamp number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a signature affixed to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature, whose signature it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander, army General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the witness has identified the document as a document coming from the general staff of the army, I would like to tender it as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in this certificate the role of the co-ordinator is clarified. Do you agree with the assessment that the role of the co-ordinator did not interfere with the hierarchical subordination role of any subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have a question that I would like to ask before the Defence counsel has asked it, because I did not identify the authenticity of this document. I merely read what was written on this document. I am not competent to determine whether the signature and the stamps are authentic, neither the number which the document has. I only read and recognised the stamp and a signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you see any indication on this document that would say that this document is not an authentic one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an officer of the army of the Federation and I am not competent to analyse the authenticity that my Commander had signed. There is an institution, the records, and a custodian of the records who needed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think that I can ask the same question to the custodian of the records, but I think the General has given enough elements about the authenticity of this document. Could I ask the question to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He was making a pertinent observation, that it does not lie on him to authenticate this document. This is what he is saying, not that he does not know the author of the letter or the signature, but it is not for him to authenticate it. There is no objection to its admissibility. So it has been accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. You will certainly be able to assess that and also we will have the custodian of the records as a witness here who will be able to recognise the document. General, I would like to ask you now: is it correct, do you agree with what is spelt out in this statement; that is, that the role of the co-ordinator has got no function of authority of issuing orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to simplify this question. Do you agree, General, with this way of explaining the role of co-ordinator given by the army General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no right to agree with the statements made by the commander. My right is either to execute his order or to agree -- this is a text, I cannot say whether it is authentic. This is a text coming from the general staff. The number here on it is the Commander's number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I hope that we will not need to ask the Commander to come, but as if you -- as you have answered, exactly, in an identical way, what is a co-ordinator, identical to what is said in this certificate I will not insist upon that. Your Honours, as it is 4 o'clock now do you think this would be an appropriate moment for our afternoon break? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may warn the witness that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is quite late in the afternoon by now and you are probably tired, just as I am, so I will try to ask very simple questions. It was slightly tense before the break, but this has probably disappeared now. I will try to proceed in the same way as my colleague Mr. Niemann did. I will show you a document and I do not ask you to authenticate a particular document. General, you have answered several questions asked by the Prosecutor concerning the competencies of a Tactical Group. If you allow me to say, all my knowledge in that area is very modest but I would nevertheless like to ask you several questions. In answer to questions put by the Prosecutor and by my colleagues you have confirmed that a Tactical Group is a temporary military formation with a particular military mission, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, before the war you also taught at the military academy, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, General, you are certainly aware of the fact that in the Yugoslav People's Army there were Brigades, the rules of the Brigade and there was a definition of a Tactical Group which is also to be found in the military encyclopaedia of the former Yugoslavia, do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, would you allow Ms. McMurrey to be excused from the courtroom for a few minutes? She has an urgent matter to take care of outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: She is excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the usher to show you, General, the excerpts from the rules of Brigades from the military encyclopaedia so that you can look at them and so that I could ask you certain questions about the contents. You can identify that, but the for the moment the Defence do not intend to tender it as evidence, but within disclosure the Defence has given these documents to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D76/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is probably also a French translation here, but please look at just the paragraph on the top of the page, page 606, where the heading is "Tactical Group". Did you have a chance to look at the top paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on page 606.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from what you had already confirmed when speaking about a Tactical Group, I would like to ask you, is it true that a Tactical Group, as it is written, here operates along special tactical lines. Is that one of the characteristics of a Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, in a general sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This general assertion -- you can, both as a teacher and as a professional soldier, you can confirm that this is a generally accepted notion in the armies in Europe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can also confirm, General, that these general rules were also applied in our army, since its very beginning, and together with a structure of the army it was also accepted as -- they were also accepted as special document of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are these general rules which were applied in the JNA, were they also accepted as rules for behaviour of our army, in making?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were all trained in the former JNA we used that knowledge also in this war and applied these principles regarding to procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as temporary and provisional formations for a specified military mission, is it true that Tactical Groups have precisely those competencies that are given to them when they are established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the definition here and all the general definitions of Tactical Groups, it is clearly stated when in general a Tactical Group is formed, but the competencies and the responsibilities of the Tactical Group are determined by the one who establishes that Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a full answer. But before going on about Tactical Groups, allow me to ask you a different question. Territorial Defence was organised before the war in companies, in municipalities, regions and in republic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regional headquarters were the bodies which were superior to municipals, to municipal headquarters, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm, General, the Tactical Groups, according to their basic purpose, their definition and the way of performing their missions, have not the same duties as the municipal headquarters, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also Tactical Groups that act along certain lines have not the same functions as a Corps does?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that a Tactical Group 1 was formed already in May 1992 with the mission of trying to lift the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that Tactical Group 1 was formed. I knew which were the units and what areas that became part of Tactical Group 1, but I am not aware of the duties and mission that the Tactical Group 1 was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know that the first Commander of the Tactical Group 1 was Mr. Mustafa Polutak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Mustafa Polutak was replaced as Commander of the Tactical Group by Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that they were all appointed according to an order of appointment by the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were appointed by the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that the headquarters of the Tactical Group 1 were at Pazaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the lines of action of this Tactical Group, this line, was Dreznica, Jablanica, Konjic, Prozor, Hadzici, Igman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall the order by which the Tactical Group was established, its Commander was appointed and also the units which were to become parts of the Tactical Group. These were the units from Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor and I also think the unit from Gornji Vakuf. As for the missions and the lines of actions, I did not know of those, about their specific missions and lines of action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that the mission of this Tactical Group and of other Tactical Groups that were formed in the siege of Sarajevo, that their basic mission was to plan and to carry out war operations for lifting the siege of Sarajevo in breaching the blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a Commander of the 1st Mostar Brigade I also gave a number of my troops for trying to break the blockade of Sarajevo in 1992, probably a Tactical Group 1 also probably had a role to play in breaking the -- blockade around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you had very intense war action going on in Sarajevo -- in Mostar at that time, could you confirm that the first time it was tried to break the siege of Sarajevo from Pazaric and Hadzici was carried out in June 1992 when the Commander of the 1st Tactical Group was Mr. Polutak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I do not know the details. I think it was called JUD, but I never knew the details, the line of action, the way they were conducting the operation. I only know that Polutak was the head of the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday, as an answer to the question of my learned colleague Mr. Niemann, you said that a part of the unit from a certain line is included into a Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what I said?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have confirmed that into Tactical Groups parts of units from a given line, that is from a given area, becomes part of a Tactical Group, for example detachments and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if we establish a Tactical Group along certain lines in a certain area then all the units that are on those lines take part in it and maybe some other units are there to it. It really depends on the forces we need for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it then true, General, that these -- the composition of these units, be it Brigades or platoons or detachments, which are added from municipal staffs to municipal headquarters to a Tactical Group that they are subordinate to the Commander of a Tactical Group for the performing of a particular mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it then true, General, that the Commander of a Tactical Group has the responsibility towards these units which are subordinate to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If certain units become part of a Tactical Group, those units with their Commanders need to be subordinate to the Tactical Group and the Commander of that Tactical Group, otherwise he would not lead the Group. He could not lead the Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, all the other units in that area that are not subordinate to the Commander of the Tactical Group remain normally under the command of the municipal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they have not made, become part of a Tactical Group then they are not part of a Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, I do not know if it is appropriate each time to point out these problems, maybe somebody could advise me. It is line 8, page 114 it says "sub board nature"; the actual word was "subordinate". I do not know whether these get caught later in the process, or whether it is necessary for us to rise and point them out. But the word is "subordinate". What was actually said was "subordinate".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That does not mean anything. I am sure that anybody reading it will know. Perhaps by the time we rise most of these things have been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Should we continue to point these out? Is that important or appropriate? I am a bit uncertain about whether I need to do that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think it is -- most of yours were good, but some of these irregularities are not as damaging as one would say, because I think "sub board nature" will mean nothing to anybody reading it. You will know it is "subordinate".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you have said that somewhere in the second half of the summer, together with General Agotic, somewhere on the front-line, you met Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Could you please tell me whether it is true that operational missions concerning lifting the siege of Sarajevo were done in the areas of Igman, Pasarici and other places which are surrounding Sarajevo and which are at a considerable distance from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Mr. Imre Agotic, who was the Chief of Staff of the HVO, we went to Konjic and we went to the front where Mr. Delalic was and that was to the east of Konjic. These were, I think, artillery positions. It is possible that in breaking the blockade of Sarajevo participate also units from a broader area, because they can try to draw the enemy's attention away from the town. So we met Zejnil Delalic and we discussed general issues of defence needed in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, as we are not going to look at the map now, could you nevertheless, as a soldier who spent the whole war in the areas of most intense fighting, could you say in front of this Trial Chamber that the areas around Sarajevo from where it was tried to break the blockade of Sarajevo, that means the areas to the south like Igman and Pazaric that are more than 60 kilometres away from the town of Konjic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact distance, but they should be somewhere at that distance, both Pasarici and Igman from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would now like to ask you something different. I am not aware whether I can ask general military questions, but nevertheless I will try to be as clear as possible. Can you tell me, General, whether it is true that every superior officer in the army who has very concrete specified duties that are linked to his function, be they as the function of the leader or the function of a Commander, he can from his superior officer receive an order to perform another military mission not directly linked to his function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such a duty can be ordered, but I do not know how that person can carry that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know Mr. Asim Dzambasovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to give you one example. Mr. Asim Dzambasovic had a very concrete duty and very concrete task, but at a certain moment from his superior officer, let us say the Chief of Staff, he received the order to be the staff Commander. For example, if he was in charge of the headquarters of the JNA, can he perform such supplementary duty without being detrimental to his basic duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a Commander if I give an order to my subordinate I have to think whether he would be able to carry out that particular mission whilst carrying out his regular duties. You always know which are the basic duties, and you can give additional duties if those additional duties are not detrimental to the performing of the basic duties. In this concrete case, I could not assess whether that was detrimental to Dzambasovic's basic functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know well that I have brought up this example because you are familiar with it and I know that it is true, but I would not like to discuss here the duties of Mr. Dzambasovic. I would like to ask you certain questions concerning Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I would like to ask you now to look at certain decisions and at certain appointments. I do not expect from you to check the contents of the documents, but I would like to ask you later on about the contents of these documents. So I would like to ask that these decisions be distributed to the Trial Chamber and to the General. I have also got the translations here. These are the documents that we received as part of disclosure from the Prosecution as documents of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The decision is marked 76/1 and the second one D78/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, have you looked at these documents? These are two documents. The first is a decision and the other is an appointment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you, please, look first at the decision? Do you see that it is a decision issued by the Supreme Command of the armed forces, Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
